content: If the contraceptive patch is used for more than 7 days but less than or equal to 9 days during weeks 2 or 3 of the cycle, while the woman is using the first or second patch, the patch should be removed or replaced as soon as possible. The woman should maintain the same patch change day and use condoms or abstain from sexual intercourse until she has worn a patch for 7 consecutive days. If the patch is used for more than 9 days during the third week of the cycle, the patch should be removed immediately, and the same patch start day should be maintained. No additional contraceptive protection is required. If the contraceptive vaginal ring (CVR) is removed for less than or equal to 48 hours at an unscheduled time, it should be reinserted as soon as possible, and the woman should keep the CVR in place until the originally scheduled removal day. No additional contraceptive protection is needed. If the CVR is removed for more than 48 hours at an unscheduled time, it should be reinserted as soon as possible. The woman should use condoms or abstain from sexual intercourse until the CVR has been worn for 7 consecutive days. If the unscheduled removal occurs during the third week of CVR use, the hormone-free week should be omitted, and a new CVR should be inserted immediately after completing the third week. If a new CVR cannot be started immediately, the woman should use condoms or abstain from sexual intercourse until the CVR has been worn for 7 consecutive days. If the CVR is used for up to 28 days (less than 4 weeks), no additional contraceptive protection is needed. A hormone-free interval of up to 7 days can be taken if desired. If the CVR is used for 28–35 days (4–5 weeks), a new CVR should be inserted immediately, skipping the hormone-free interval. No additional contraceptive protection is required. For combined injectable contraceptives (CICs), the first injection can be given within 7 days of the start of menstrual bleeding without requiring additional contraceptive protection. If more than 7 days have passed since the start of menstrual bleeding, the injection can still be given if it is reasonably certain the woman is not pregnant, but she will need to abstain from sex or use additional contraceptive protection for the next 7 days. For postpartum women who are breastfeeding, CICs should not be used within the first 6 weeks postpartum. Between 6 weeks and 6 months postpartum, CICs are generally not recommended unless no other methods are available. After 6 months postpartum, the first injection can be given as advised for other amenorrheic women or those with returned menstrual cycles. For postpartum women who are not breastfeeding, CICs are generally not recommended within the first 21 days postpartum unless no other methods are available. After 21 days, the first injection can be given if it is reasonably certain the woman is not pregnant, with additional contraceptive protection required for the next 7 days if menstrual cycles have not returned. For post-abortion women, the first CIC injection can be given immediately without requiring additional contraceptive protection. When switching from another hormonal method, the first CIC injection can be given immediately if the previous method was used consistently and correctly, or if it is reasonably certain the woman is not pregnant. No additional contraceptive protection is needed. When switching from an intrauterine device (IUD), the first CIC injection can be given within 7 days of the start of menstrual bleeding without requiring additional contraceptive protection. If more than 7 days have passed, the injection can still be given if it is reasonably certain the woman is not pregnant, but additional contraceptive protection will be needed for the next 7 days. If the woman is sexually active in the current cycle, the IUD should be left in place until the next menstrual period. For repeat CIC injections, they should be administered every 4 weeks. If the injection is late by up to 7 days, no additional contraceptive protection is needed. If the injection is more than 7 days late, the woman should abstain from sex or use additional contraceptive protection for the next 7 days and may consider emergency contraception if appropriate. Blood pressure screening is desirable before initiating CICs, but women should not be denied access to CICs if blood pressure measurements are unavailable, especially in settings with high pregnancy-related risks.
